title: The 4-Part Prompt That Ends Vague AI Answers

beats.text: Most people talk to AI like they are texting a friend. Then they wonder why the answer is so vague.

msgs.text: Sure! Here is a *generic* paragraph about product launches in general...

beats.text: There is a simple fix. Four parts, in this order. Role, context, task, and format.
Part one is the role. Tell the model who to be. An editor answers very differently than a salesperson.

scene.title: prompt.txt
lines: Role: You are a senior editor at a tech magazine.
You value short sentences, plain words,

beats.text: Part two is context. Give it the facts it cannot guess. Who will read this, and what do they already know?

scene.title: prompt.txt
lines: Role: You are a senior editor at a tech magazine.
Context: The reader is a [busy manager].
They know the product, not the new feature.
The launch email goes out on Friday.

beats.text: Part three is the task. One clear verb, one clear job. Summarise, compare, or rewrite. Not all three at once.
Part four is the format. Say exactly what you want back. A table, five bullets, or a short email.
Put it together, and the same request becomes a complete brief. Now look at the reply.

msgs.text: Role: senior editor. Context: busy manager. Task: *rewrite* these notes. Format: email, under 120 words.
Subject: What changes on Friday. Hi team, three things to know before the launch...

beats.text: The difference shows up in the rewrites. A one-line prompt often needs several rounds. A full brief usually needs fewer.
This is also why longer prompts win. Not because length matters, but because every part removes one guess.
Two habits make it even stronger. Ask the model to check its answer against your facts. And always read it before you send.
So here is the checklist to save: role, context, task, and format.
Try it on your next email, and see how many guesses disappear.
